title: The Hidden Rabies Risk in Vietnam's Unregulated Dog Meat Trade
excerpt: Informal slaughter practices create direct exposure pathways for rabies and other zoonotic diseases. Without regulated facilities, the risk to workers and consumers remains unquantified and unmanaged.
body_html:
Vietnam's dog meat trade operates entirely outside the formal food safety system. There are zero registered slaughterhouses — meaning no inspections, no safety protocols, and no disease screening at any point in the supply chain.

Rabies is the most acute risk. Dogs transported long distances under extreme stress show suppressed immune responses, and informal slaughter conditions — often involving blunt force — create direct blood and saliva exposure for workers and bystanders. The Ho Chi Minh City Food Safety Management Authority has issued multiple consumption warnings in recent years, citing these exact pathways.

E. coli and Salmonella contamination are also endemic in unregulated meat handling environments. Without refrigeration, sanitation, or inspection, contamination rates in informal dog meat markets are significantly higher than in regulated meat sectors.

This is not a marginal issue. With an estimated 5 million dogs entering the trade annually, the scale of unregulated meat handling represents a genuine and ongoing public health risk — one that receives far less attention than it deserves.

95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending this trade — and the public health argument is one of the strongest reasons why. Sign the petition to demand regulated food safety standards and a permanent ban.
author: SDE Research Team
